entry.title: Untitled 3
entry.content:
The slice angles form a geometric sequence $a_n$, with common ratio $r = 1.22$, and the initial term $a_0=10$.

Let the number of slices be $n$. Then

$$10(\frac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}) = 10 ( 1 + r + \ldots + r^{n-1} ) =\ \rm total\ angle$$

Here the total angle is of that of the circular cake, which is 360 degree.

Rearrangement gives $n = \frac{\ln [ (r - 1 ) ({\rm \ total\ angle }/10) + 1 ]}{\ln r} = 11.0047... \approx 11$

In the slices, the taken ones are the 4th and 8th.

The angle of the 4th: $a_3 = 10 \cdot r ^3$.

THe anlge of the 8th: $a_7 = 10 \cdot r^4$.

The total angles taken:

$${\rm taken\ } = 10 \times (r^3 + r^7) \approx 147.50209$$

So the remaining area is:

$$\pi r^2 \times \left ( 1 - {\rm taken\ } / 360\right) \approx 65$$
.

  • 8.1.2 Prove that the real projective space $P^n$ is a manifold by constructing, for any $0\leq i\leq n$, a homeomorphism between the subset
    $$U_i = \{\text{span}\{(x_0,x_1, \ldots, x_n )\} \colon x_i \neq 0 \} \subset P^n$$
    and $\mathbb R^n$. Similarly, prove that the complex projective space is also a manifold.

Relevant Definitions. We denote space spanned by the vector $(x_1,\dots, x_n)$ with thenotation $[x_1: \dots : x_n]$. This definition implies that $[\lambda x_1 : \dots : \lambda x_n] = [x_1 : \dots : x_n]$. The real linear projective space $P^n$ is the set of $1$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\mathbb R^n$. Let $\phi\colon \mathbb R^n \to P^n$, $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto [x_1:\dots:x_n]$. A set $V \in P^n$ is open if and only $\phi^{-1}(V)$ is open, by the definition of the topology of $P^n$.

Answer.
We will use the universal properties of the subspace and quotient topology.
In this proof, there is not much geometries going on; instead everything is just
the application of the universal properties.

Let $S=:\mathbb R^n \setminus \{0\} - \{(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\in \mathbb R^n | v_i = 0\}$.
We endow $S$ with the subspace topology of $\mathbb R^n$. Also, the quotient map restricted on $S$ has the image $U_i$. Hence $\pi\colon : S \to U_i$ is well defined.
Since $f\colon S\to \mathbb R^n$, $(v_1, \ldots, v_n) \to (\frac{v_1}{v_i}, \ldots, \frac{v_n}{v_i})$ is a map such that $f(x) = f(y) \iff \exists \lambda \in \mathbb R \,s.t. \, x=\lambda y \iff \pi(x)=\pi(y)$, there exists a unique map $g\colon U_i \to \mathbb R^{n-1}$ such that $f=g\circ \pi$. This map $f$ is given by $[v_1: \dots : v_i : \dots : v_n] \mapsto (v_1, \ldots , v_n)$.

Now, $g$ is continuous if and only if $f$ is continuous. Is $f$ continuous? The inclusion
map $\iota_S: S\to \mathbb R^n$ is certainly continuous. Also, the inclusion map $\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{n-1}} \to \mathbb R^n$ is continuous. Since $\iota_S = \iota_{\mathbb R^{n-1}} \circ f$, we know that $f$ is continuous, by the universal property of the subspace $\mathbb R^{n-1} \subset \mathbb R^n$. So, it follows that $g$ is continuous.

We need to show that the reverse of $g$ is continuous as well. It decomposes to a composition of continuous maps:

$$\mathbb R^{n-1} \quad \overset{(v_1, \ldots, v_n) \mapsto (v_1, \ldots, 1, \ldots ,v_n)}{\to} \quad S \overset{\pi}{\to} U_i$$
.

entry.title: sums
entry.content:
Estimation of Summations

$\frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{k=1} n^{1/k}$

By plotting, you can find that the $\frac{1}{n} \sum^\infty_{k=1} k^{1/k}$ finally goes to $1$, because $\{k^{1/k}\} \to 1$, from which the average goes to $1$ by Cesaro-Stolz lemma.
Now replacing this sum by $\frac{1}{n} \sum^\infty_{k=1} n^{1/k}$, it helps to
estimate the new summation by splitting the sum into two pieces.

The summation is

$$n + n^{1/2} + n^{1/3} + \ldots n^{1/n}.$$

The first $\ln(n)$ terms can be estimated by summing $\sqrt n$.

Why would the upper bound $n^{1/k} \leq \sqrt n$ for the first $\ln(n)$ work?? The reason is that we know the sum
$\sum_{2 \leq k < \ln n} n^{1/k} \leq \ln(n) \sqrt n = o(n)$ as $n\to\infty$, and so this upper bound is sufficient.

Now we estimate $\sum_{\ln n \leq k \leq n} n^{1/k}$.

Inequality

The first inequality to use is

$$e^{\ln n /k} \leq 3\frac{\ln n}{k} + 1$$
for $k\geq \ln n$. ($e^x < 3 \implies e^x < 3x +1$ for $x\in [0,1]$)

Also, for $k \geq 2$,

$$1/k = \int^{k}_{k-1} \frac{1}{k} dt <\int^{k}_{k-1} \frac{1}{t} dt$$

So

$$\sum^n_{k=2} 1/k < \sum^n_{k=2} \int^k_{k-1} \frac{1}{t}dt = \int^n_{1} \frac{1}{t}dt =\ln n \tag{1}$$

Concluding Estimate

$$\sum_{\ln n < k \leq n} n^{1/k} = \sum_{\ln n < k \leq n} e^{\ln n/k} < 3 \ln n \left(\sum^n_{k=2} \frac{1}{k}\right) + n< 3\ln n \ln n + n = o(n) + n$$

Here we used the fact that $\ln^j(n) = o(n^k)$ for all positive $j,k$.

Comments

A key step in the estimation above is $e^x < 3x +1$ for $x\in [0,1]$, which is actually a quite precise one.
Generally, if $f(x)$ is convex on $[a, \infty)$, then $f(x)< Kx + D$ for $x\in (a,\infty)$, where $K=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ and $D=f(a)-Ka$. As a result,

$$\sum_{a\leq x \leq n} f(x) = \underbrace{K\sum_{a\leq x \leq n} x}_{(1)} + \underbrace{Dn}_{(2)}$$
Note that when $a>1$, (1) is $O(n^2)$ while $(2)$ is $O(n)$. They are not able to become a constant by letting be divided by a power of $n$. However, when $x\in (0,1)$ and $a\leq 0$, we can possibly make (1) of the magnitude $o(n)$.

Related Questions

  1. $$\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{n}\sum^n_{k=1} \sin\left(\frac{n}{k}\right)$$

Also think about this problem when the argument of $\sin$ is $k/n$ instead of $n/k$.
This is a Riemann sum.

$$\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{\ln n < k\leq n} \exp(n/k)$$

This is a Riemann sum.
3.

$$\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{n}\sum^n_{k=1} \exp\bigg(\frac{\ln\ln n}{k}\bigg)$$

Solution. $\exp(\frac{\ln\ln n}{k}) = (\ln n)^{1/k}$. So $\sum \exp\bigg(\frac{\ln\ln n}{k}\bigg) = \sum (\ln n)^{1/k}$
The first piece of sum is $\sum_{1\leq k \leq \ln \ln n} (\ln n)^{1/k} \leq \ln\ln n (\ln n) = o(n)$
Note that for $x\in(0,1)$, $1\leq e^x \leq 1+ 2x$.
The second piece of the sum is
$$\sum_{\ln\ln n < k \leq n} (\ln n)^{1/k} \approx\sum_{\ln\ln n < k \leq n} \left( 1 + \ln\ln n (\frac{1}{k})\right)\leq n + \ln\ln n\bigg(\sum^n_{k=1} \frac{1}{k}\bigg)= n + \ln\ln (n) (\ln n)=n + o(n)$$
So the whole sum is $n+ o(n)$. Q.E.D.
Comment This proof splits the sum when $x$ in $e^x$ is greater than 1 than when it is less than 1. So, the key there is still the inequality $1\leq e^x \leq 1 +2x$. It is evident that, to make this average approach $1$ when $n\to \infty$, the choice of function $f(x)$ in the expression $f(x))^{1/k}$ is unessential.

  1. $$\sum^n_{k=1}\frac{1}{k^2}$$

entry.title: sequences_series
entry.content:
1. Is
    $$\frac{1}{1 + z^n}$$
    convergent or divergent for complex number $z$?

Hints. Comparison test for positive series: Suppose $\{a_n\}$ and $\{b_n\}$ are positive series. If $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = A (\neq 0)$, then $\sum a_n$ and $\sum b_n$ simutaneously convergent or divergent.
Term Test: If $\sum a_n$ is convergent, then $\lim_{n\to \infty}a_n =0$.

Solution. If $|z|\leq 1$, then

$$\left|\frac{1}{1 + z^n}\right| \geq \frac{1}{|1| + |z^n|} = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}.$$
So $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + x^n}\neq 0$. So this series diverges for $|z|=1$. If $|z| >1$, then $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{z^n}} = 1$. Let $b_n = \frac{1}{z^n}$. The series $\sum \frac{1}{1 + z^n}$ converges because
$$\lim \bigg(\frac{1}{1 + z^n}\bigg) \bigg/b_n = \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{z^n}} = 1$$
from which the comparison test confirms the convergence. $\square$
